label: holy roman empire

Acquired in 1198 by the noble Lupi family, the lordship was centred upon the heavily fortified stronghold of Rocca Meli Lupi. The rulers successfully navigated complex regional rivalries between the Guelph communes of Piacenza and Cremona and the Ghibelline lords of Lombardy, maintaining imperial immediacy and local jurisdiction until Holy Roman Emperor Charles IV elevated Soragna to an imperial marquisate in 1347. \n\n Status: Signoria; Capital: Soragna; Common languages: Emilian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruling dynasty: Lupi family; Historical era: High to Late Middle Ages; Established: 1198; Disestablished: 1347; Succeeded by: Marquisate of Soragna

name: Commune of Assisi

name: Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia

name: Arakkal Kingdom

name: Bono State

name: Commune of Aulla

name: Commune of Castiglione della Pescaia
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Castiglione della Pescaia was an autonomous coastal municipality situated in the southern Tuscan Maremma along the Tyrrhenian Sea. Castiglione maintained its republican autonomy until the naval and military expansion of the Republic of Pisa annexed the town in 1275. \n\n Status: Free commune; Capital: Castiglione della Pescaia; Common languages: Tuscan Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Communal republic; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1200; Disestablished: 1275; Succeeded by: Republic of Pisa

name: Commune of Cortona

Cortona aligned itself with the Ghibelline cause during regional Tuscan conflicts, successfully repelling aggression from neighbouring Guelph Arezzo and Perugia. name: Commune of Fano

Fano defended its civic freedoms through alliances with the Lombard League and regional pacts, engaging in bitter territorial rivalries with neighbouring Pesaro and Senigallia until internal factional strife allowed the Malatesta dynasty of Rimini to establish signorial control. \n\n Status: Free commune; Capital: Fano; Common languages: Marchigiano Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Communal republic; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1201; Disestablished: 1301; Succeeded by: Signoria of Malatesta

name: Commune of Monza
label: holy roman empire

name: Magba

name: Vaghela Dynasty

name: Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia

label: holy roman empire

name: Principality of Hlukhiv

name: Kingdom of Eastern Georgia

name: Sultanate of Egypt

The Mamluk sultans protected the Islamic holy sanctuaries in Mecca and Medina, presiding over an era of architectural grandeur and international commerce until the Ottoman conquest. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Cairo; Official languages: Arabic; Common languages: Arabic and Kipchak Turkic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Stratocratic elective monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Ayyubid dynasty; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Commune of Savignone

name: County of Eschenlohe
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Eschenlohe was an imperial comital lordship situated along the Loisach River at the foot of the Bavarian Alps. Held by the noble Eschenlohe dynasty, the estate exercised judicial authority over alpine valleys, timber reserves and strategic transit corridors linking Augsburg with northern Italy. Facing mounting financial difficulties and lack of male heirs, the counts gradually alienated their seigneurial rights to the neighbouring prince-bishoprics of Augsburg and Freising. \n\n Status: Imperial county; Capital: Eschenlohe; Common languages: Bavarian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal county; Ruling dynasty: House of Eschenlohe; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Prince-Bishopric of Freising

name: County of Sigmaringen
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Sigmaringen was a medieval feudal estate of the Holy Roman Empire established along the upper Danube River in southern Swabia. Centred on the imposing rock castle of Sigmaringen, the ruling comital line wielded judicial and territorial jurisdiction across surrounding river valleys and farming communities. The county tenaciously preserved its seigneurial prerogatives against neighbouring Swabian magnates until dynastic transfers conveyed the territory to the counts of Württemberg and later Hohenzollern. \n\n Status: Imperial county; Capital: Sigmaringen; Common languages: Swabian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Historical region: Swabia; Succeeded by: County of Württemberg

name: Free Imperial City of Buchau

name: Free Imperial City of Esslingen
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Esslingen was a prosperous self-governing civic republic of the Holy Roman Empire located along the Neckar River in central Swabia. Esslingen steadfastly defended its civic liberties against persistent annexation attempts by the neighbouring counts of Württemberg for over five hundred years. \n\n Status: Free imperial city; Capital: Esslingen am Neckar; Common languages: Swabian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Oligarchic city council; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Preceded by: Duchy of Swabia; Succeeded by: Duchy of Württemberg

name: Free Imperial City of Toul
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Toul was an autonomous urban commune of the Holy Roman Empire located along the Moselle River in Lorraine. After freeing itself from episcopal administration through imperial privilege, the city governed its domestic affairs through elected aldermen and defended its municipal ramparts. Toul preserved its political liberties within the Three Bishoprics until French military forces occupied the enclave in 1552, formalising French control under the Peace of Westphalia. \n\n Status: Free imperial city; Capital: Toul; Common languages: French and Lorraine Franconian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Municipal commune; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France

name: Kingdom of Dagbon
description: The Kingdom of Dagbon was an influential West African traditional state established across the savannah plains of northern modern Ghana by the Dagomba people. Founded under the leadership of Naa Gbewaa, the kingdom established a centralised monarchy where the paramount ruler, the Yaa Naa, governed alongside traditional earth priests known as Tindaamba. Dagbon developed sophisticated cavalry forces, intricate chieftaincy hierarchies and oral court traditions that sustained the kingdom across centuries of regional commerce. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Yendi; Common languages: Dagbani; Religion: Traditional African religion and Sunni Islam; Government: Centralised traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Yaa Naa; First ruler: Naa Gbewaa; Historical era: High Middle Ages

name: Kingdom of Wolaita
description: The Kingdom of Wolaita was an independent traditional monarchy established by the Omotic-speaking Wolayta people in the fertile highlands of southern Ethiopia. Governed by sacred hereditary monarchs known as the Kawos, the kingdom organised intensive terrace farming, built elaborate defensive earthworks and maintained distinct courtly institutions. Wolaita vigorously safeguarded its political autonomy and cultural traditions against expanding northern empires and nomadic incursions until its conquest in the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Sodo; Common languages: Wolaytta; Religion: Traditional beliefs and Ethiopian Christianity; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Kawo; First ruler: Motolomi Sato; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Ethiopian Empire

name: Lathi State
description: Lathi State was a small princely state situated in the Kathiawar peninsula of modern Gujarat, founded by Sarangji of the Gohil Rajput clan. Originating as an autonomous appanage following the division of Gohil tribal territories, the ruling Thakurs governed agricultural lands and local trade routes from their fortified seat at Lathi. The principality preserved its hereditary governance and martial traditions through centuries of regional upheaval before entering into subsidiary alliance with the British Empire. \n\n Status: Autonomous princely state; Capital: Lathi; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Gohil dynasty; Ruler title: Thakur; First ruler: Sarangji; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Historical region: Saurashtra

name: Lordship of Mindelheim
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Mindelheim was an imperial barony of the Holy Roman Empire located along the Mindel River in the Bavarian region of Swabia. name: Paramountcy of Samoa

name: Kingdom of Lithuania
description: The Kingdom of Lithuania was a sovereign Baltic monarchy established when Duke Mindaugas received a royal crown with the blessing of Pope Innocent IV in 1251. Mindaugas's conversion to Roman Catholicism and subsequent coronation elevated Lithuania into the Christian commonwealth of European kingdoms, temporarily deterring Teutonic and Livonian crusader attacks. Following internal dynastic strife and Mindaugas's assassination in 1263, the realm reverted to pagan traditions and transformed into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Vilnius; Common languages: Lithuanian and Ruthenian; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Baltic paganism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Mindaugas; Ruler title: King; First ruler: Mindaugas; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Preceded by: Duchy of Lithuania; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

name: Free Imperial City of Mühlhausen
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Mühlhausen was an autonomous urban republic of the Holy Roman Empire situated along the Unstrut River in north-western Thuringia. Holding imperial immediacy from the mid-thirteenth century, the prosperous municipality was administered by a patrician council that directed extensive regional cloth trade and agrarian estates. Mühlhausen successfully defended its fortified perimeter and municipal exemptions against encroaching regional landgraves until its mediatisation to Prussia in 1803. \n\n Status: Free imperial city; Capital: Mühlhausen; Common languages: German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Patrician city council; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Prussia

name: Commune of Montalcino
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Montalcino was an autonomous medieval city-state perched on a fortified volcanic ridge overlooking the Val d'Orcia in southern Tuscany. Governing fertile hill slopes renowned for viticulture and olive farming, the municipal council guarded its local statutes through shifting tactical alliances with Siena and Florence. Montalcino's brief period of full civic sovereignty concluded when escalating regional conflicts forced the town to submit to Sienese territorial authority. \n\n Status: City-state commune; Capital: Montalcino; Common languages: Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Civic republic; Ruler title: Podesta; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Republic of Siena

name: Free Imperial City of Friedberg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Friedberg was an autonomous civic republic of the Holy Roman Empire located in the fertile Wetterau plain north of Frankfurt. Granted imperial immediacy by the Hohenstaufen emperors, the merchant town governed its craft guilds and lucrative livestock fairs while defending its walls independently of the adjacent Friedberg Castle garrison. The city preserved its communal rights and imperial judicial status until it was mediatised into the Grand Duchy of Hesse. \n\n Status: Free imperial city; Capital: Friedberg; Common languages: German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Civic council; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Preceded by: Duchy of Franconia; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Hesse

name: Commune of Crocefieschi
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Crocefieschi was an autonomous medieval highland community situated among the jagged Apennine peaks of the upper Scrivia basin in northern Liguria. Administered by local communal elders, the settlement commanded steep mule trails that connected coastal Genoese trade with the inland agricultural centres of the Po basin. The commune protected its customary grazing rights and mountain tolls until it was formally absorbed into the aristocratic feudatory domains of the Fieschi family. \n\n Status: Rural commune; Capital: Crocefieschi; Common languages: Ligurian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Municipal commune; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Historical region: Liguria; Succeeded by: Republic of Genoa

name: Dali Kingdom
description: The Dali Kingdom was a Bai-dominated realm in modern Yunnan that became a tributary vassal under the Mongol Empire following the decisive invasion led by Kublai Khan in 1253. Although the conquest terminated the sovereign imperial lineage of the Duan family, Mongol administrators retained the native monarchs as hereditary military governors or tusi. The kingdom retained its distinctive Buddhist culture and local administrative machinery while providing logistical support and auxiliary troops for Mongol campaigns in Southeast Asia. \n\n Status: Mongol vassal kingdom; Capital: Dali; Common languages: Bai and Literary Chinese; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Monarchy under imperial tusi administration; Ruling dynasty: Duan dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Preceded by: Dali Kingdom

name: Kingdom of Rus'
description: The Kingdom of Rus' was the western East Slavic monarchy formed when Prince Daniel of Galicia accepted a royal crown from Pope Innocent IV at Dorohochyn while maintaining nominal vassalage under the Mongol Empire. Daniel sought European ecclesiastical recognition and military assistance to assemble an anti-Mongol coalition capable of defending Halych and Volhynia. Despite this royal elevation, the kingdom remained subject to Mongol tributary demands and punitive oversight from Sarai during this transitional phase. \n\n Status: Mongol vassal kingdom; Capital: Halych; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Ruler title: King; First ruler: Daniel of Galicia; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia

name: Usfurids
description: The Usfurids were an autonomous Arab dynastic principality that established hegemony across eastern Arabia and the Bahrain archipelago after overthrowing the Uyunid Emirate in 1253. Tracing their ancestry to the Banu Uqayl tribe, the rulers governed rich date palm oases and lucrative Persian Gulf pearl fisheries from their regional centre at al-Ahsa. The dynasty maintained maritime trading routes linking southern Mesopotamia with the Arabian Sea while resisting incursions by neighbouring Persian Gulf rulers. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Al-Ahsa; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Shia Islam; Government: Dynastic emirate; Ruling dynasty: Usfurid dynasty; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Preceded by: Uyunid Emirate; Succeeded by: Jarwanid dynasty

name: Commune of Foligno
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Foligno was an independent medieval city-state situated on the Topino River within the fertile central plain of Umbria. Benefiting from its position at the crossroads of key trans-Apennine commercial highways, the civic commune developed robust woollen cloth manufacturing and established municipal legislative councils. Foligno fiercely defended its communal liberties against neighbouring Perugia and Assisi before transitioning into an aristocratic signoria under the Trinci family. \n\n Status: City-state commune; Capital: Foligno; Common languages: Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Civic republic; Ruler title: Podesta; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Historical region: Umbria; Succeeded by: Signoria of Foligno

name: County of Loano
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Loano was an autonomous imperial fief of the Holy Roman Empire situated along the western Ligurian Riviera between Albenga and Savona. Established around a fortified coastal stronghold and governed by a cadet branch of the prominent Doria family of Genoa, the miniature state exercised sovereign fiscal and minting privileges. Loano guarded its distinct territorial status as an independent enclave amidst Genoese lands until dynastic agreements transferred the territory to the House of Savoy. \n\n Status: Imperial county; Capital: Loano; Common languages: Ligurian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Doria family; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Sardinia

name: Sant State
description: Sant State was an autonomous Hindu princely state situated in the rugged, forested frontier hills of eastern Gujarat, founded by the Mahipavat branch of the Paramara Rajput dynasty. Operating from their fortified capital at Santrampur, the ruling rajas maintained defensive control over strategic river passes bordering Malwa and Mewar. The principality sustained its hereditary governance and distinct martial identity through centuries of regional instability before concluding a treaty of subsidiary alliance with the British Crown. \n\n Status: Autonomous princely state; Capital: Santrampur; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Paramara dynasty; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Bombay Presidency

name: East Breifne
label: irish medieval kingdoms;celtic polities
description: East Breifne, historically known as Breifne O'Reilly, was an independent Gaelic kingdom established across County Cavan following the territorial partition of the ancient Kingdom of Breifne in 1256. Ruled by the Ó Raghallaigh dynasty from their lakeside strongholds at Belturbet and Cavan, the kingdom maintained traditional Brehon laws, pastoral cattle economies and elective royal succession. The realm defended its independence against Anglo-Norman expansion for centuries until English authorities shired the territory into Ulster. \n\n Status: Gaelic kingdom; Capital: Cavan; Common languages: Irish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Tanistry elective monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ó Raghallaigh dynasty; Ruler title: King; First ruler: Conchobar Uí Raghallaigh; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Breifne

name: Kingdom of Rus'
description: The Kingdom of Rus' entered a brief period of open defiance against Mongol dominion following King Daniel's papal coronation, actively asserting complete territorial sovereignty across Galicia and Volhynia. Daniel reorganised his armies, constructed modern stone fortresses at Danilov and Kholm, and expelled Mongol garrisons from neighbouring Podolian towns. Although this assertive bid for total independence provoked a devastating retaliatory campaign under Mongol general Burundai, the realm briefly stood as an uncompromised sovereign kingdom. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Halych; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Ruler title: King; First ruler: Daniel of Galicia; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia

name: Mong Mao State
label: shan states
description: Mong Mao State was an autonomous Tai monarchy centred along the fertile Nam Mao and Ruili river valleys along the modern borderlands of Myanmar and Yunnan. Governed by powerful hereditary saophas, the state rapidly expanded into a dominant regional mandala that incorporated surrounding Tai chiefdoms and commanded lucrative caravan routes into upper Burma. Mong Mao preserved its sovereign political integrity through skilful military deterrence and trade alliances until entering tributary relations with the Ming Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign mandala kingdom; Administrative seat: Selan; Common languages: Shan and Tai Mao; Religion: Tai folk religion and Theravada Buddhism; Government: Feudal mandala monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Si Kefa dynasty; Ruler title: Saopha; Historical era: Late Middle Ages

name: West Breifne
label: irish medieval kingdoms;celtic polities
description: West Breifne, also known as Breifne O'Rourke, was an independent Gaelic kingdom established across the rugged hill country of modern County Leitrim following the split of the historic Breifne kingdom in 1256. Ruled by the Ó Ruairc dynasty from their fortified seat at Dromahair, the kingdom preserved ancient pastoral traditions, Gaelic legal codes and fiercely defended clan territories. The realm maintained autonomy through shifting alliances with neighbouring Gaelic lords until English plantation policies confiscated the chieftaincy lands in the early seventeenth century. \n\n Status: Gaelic kingdom; Capital: Dromahair; Common languages: Irish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Tanistry elective monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ó Ruairc dynasty; Ruler title: King; First ruler: Conchobar Ó Ruairc; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Breifne

name: Free Imperial City of Haguenau
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Haguenau was an autonomous civic republic of the Holy Roman Empire located in northern Alsace along the Moder River. Bestowed with imperial immediacy by the Staufen emperors, the town became the administrative headquarters and chief member of the Alsatian Decapole, a mutual defence league of ten free cities. Haguenau operated independent municipal courts and regulated thriving agricultural trade until the territorial settlements following the Thirty Years' War brought the city under French sovereignty. \n\n Status: Free imperial city; Capital: Haguenau; Common languages: Alsatian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Civic council; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Preceded by: Duchy of Swabia; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France

name: Idar State
description: Idar State was an independent Rajput princely state situated in the rugged, rocky terrain of the Sabarkantha region in north-eastern Gujarat. Founded by the Rathore clan after dislodging earlier Koli and Bhil chieftains, the state defended its mountain redoubts from the ancient hilltop fort of Idargadh. The ruling dynasty maintained territorial autonomy through protracted resistance against neighbouring sultanates, preserving its sovereignty until the rise of the Maratha Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Idar; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rathore dynasty; Ruler title: Rao; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Maratha Empire

name: Kamata Kingdom
description: The Kamata Kingdom was an independent realm in western Kamarupa that emerged along the Brahmaputra valley across modern western Assam and northern Bengal. Established when King Sandhya relocated his administrative capital to Kamatapur following successful resistance against Delhi Sultanate incursions, the kingdom developed into a major political power of northeast India. The realm patronised regional Hindu literature, constructed vast moat systems and governed extensive agricultural plains until falling to the Bengal Sultanate. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kamatapur; Common languages: Early Assamese and Kamatapuri; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Khen dynasty; Ruler title: Kamateshwar; First ruler: Sandhya; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kamarupa Kingdom

name: Landi State
label: holy roman empire
description: Landi State was an autonomous feudal territory of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the upper Taro and Ceno valleys of the northern Apennines. Governed by the aristocratic Landi dynasty from the formidable mountain fortresses of Bardi and Compiano, the state maintained imperial immediacy and judicial sovereignty over vital trans-Apennine passes. The family preserved its fiscal exemptions and regional independence amidst the expansionist ambitions of Milan and Parma before selling its domains to the Farnese dukes. \n\n Status: Imperial fiefdom; Capital: Bardi; Common languages: Italian and Emilian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: Landi family; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Duchy of Parma

name: Sultanate of Ternate
description: The Sultanate of Ternate was an influential Islamic maritime monarchy established on the volcanic island of Ternate in the North Maluku archipelago. Originating as the Kingdom of Gapi under Kolano Momole Cico, the realm converted to Islam and leveraged its indigenous monopoly over valuable clove production to forge an extensive maritime empire. Ternate commanded fleets of war outriggers and dominated maritime spice commerce across eastern Indonesia before encountering European colonial competition. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Ternate; Common languages: Ternate and Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Maritime monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; First ruler: Baab Mashur Malamo; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Dutch East Indies

name: County of Nidda
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Nidda was a small feudal territory of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the northern Wetterau along the Nidda River in modern Hesse. Holding imperial immediacy as a fief of the Princely Abbey of Fulda, the county was ruled by an independent comital lineage from the fortified castle at Nidda. The counts exercised judicial and administrative control over local farming villages until the extinction of their male line led to the inheritance of the county by the counts of Ziegenhain. \n\n Status: Imperial county; Capital: Nidda; Common languages: German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Malsburg-Nidda; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: County of Ziegenhain

name: County of Tenda
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Tenda was an independent alpine principality situated around the strategic Col de Tende in the Maritime Alps between Piedmont and the Mediterranean coast. Founded by a branch of the Lascaris di Ventimiglia dynasty following the marriage of Count Guglielmo Pietro I to Byzantine princess Eudoxia Laskarina, the county commanded the essential Salt Road linking Nice and Turin. The realm preserved its lucrative toll revenues and feudal autonomy against Savoyard and Genoese expansion until late sixteenth-century integration into Savoy. \n\n Status: Feudal county; Capital: Tende; Common languages: Ligurian, Occitan and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Lascaris di Ventimiglia; Ruler title: Count; First ruler: Guglielmo Pietro I; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Duchy of Savoy

name: County of Tripoli
label: crusader states
description: The County of Tripoli was a prominent Crusader state in northern Lebanon that was compelled to accept tributary vassalage under the Mongol Empire in 1259. Confronted with the overwhelming advance of Mongol general Kitbuqa's forces into the Levant, Count Bohemond VI negotiated submission to preserve his coastal capital from destruction. Tripoli paid tribute and provided auxiliary Christian troops to the Mongols, alienating neighbouring Frankish barons and provoking severe military retaliation from the rising Mamluk Sultanate. \n\n Status: Mongol vassal state; Capital: Tripoli; Common languages: Old French and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Poitiers-Antioch; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Preceded by: County of Tripoli

name: Đại Việt
description: Đại Việt was a sovereign Vietnamese kingdom centred in the Red River delta that entered into a brief tributary accommodation under the Mongol Empire following the initial invasion of 1258. Under the Trần dynasty, Emperor Trần Thái Tông temporarily acknowledged Mongol suzerainty to secure the withdrawal of foreign forces and rebuild the devastated capital of Thang Long. The kingdom provided diplomatic tribute while reorganising its military defences, firmly rejecting deeper imperial submission and preparing for future Mongol conflicts. \n\n Status: Mongol tributary kingdom; Capital: Hanoi; Official languages: Literary Chinese; Common languages: Vietnamese; Religion: Mahayana Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Trần dynasty; Ruler title: Emperor; First ruler: Trần Thái Tông; Historical era: High Middle Ages

name: Maynila
label: barangay states
description: Maynila was an autonomous coastal trading kingdom situated at the mouth of the Pasig River along the eastern shores of Manila Bay in Luzon. Governed by indigenous rajahs who formed close diplomatic and mercantile ties with the Sultanate of Brunei, the settlement commanded lucrative maritime trade linking the Philippine archipelago with Song and Yuan China. Maynila operated fortified earthen ramparts armed with bronze cannons known as lantakas, maintaining commercial independence until Spanish colonisation in 1571. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Manila; Common languages: Old Tagalog and Malay; Religion: Indigenous animism and Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Rajah; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Captaincy General of the Philippines

name: Prince-Bishopric of Augsburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Prince-Bishopric of Augsburg was an ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire located in Swabia along the Lech and Danube rivers. Endowed with imperial immediacy, the prince-bishops exercised temporal authority over fragmented rural territories and castellated market towns distinct from the Free City of Augsburg. Following escalating jurisdictional disputes with the town burghers, the bishops relocated their permanent episcopal residence northwards to Dillingen an der Donau, governing until Bavarian secularisation in 1803. \n\n Status: Prince-bishopric; Capital: Augsburg; Administrative seat: Dillingen an der Donau; Common languages: Swabian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical elective principality; Ruler title: Prince-Bishop; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Electorate of Bavaria

name: Twipra Kingdom
description: The Twipra Kingdom was an independent indigenous monarchy established across the hill tracts and river plains of modern Tripura and south-eastern Bangladesh by the Tripuri people. Governed by the hereditary Manikya dynasty, the kingdom maintained its religious traditions and political sovereignty against neighbouring kingdoms and eastern Islamic conquerors. The state derived wealth from rich agricultural floodplains and trans-regional trade, preserving its cultural institutions and royal prestige across centuries of regional conflict. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Rangamati; Common languages: Kokborok and Bengali; Religion: Traditional animism and Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Manikya dynasty; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Tripura Princely State

name: Signoria of Milan
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Milan was a powerful medieval state in Lombardy that emerged when Martino della Torre was appointed lord of the city in May 1259, replacing communal governance with aristocratic dynastic rule. Following intense warfare between factional Guelf and Ghibelline elites, control passed to the Visconti dynasty after the Battle of Desio in 1277. The Visconti rulers centralised the Lombard administration, expanded territorial borders across northern Italy and transformed the signoria into the prestigious Duchy of Milan in 1395. \n\n Status: Imperial signoria; Capital: Milan; Common languages: Lombard and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Signorial autocracy; Ruling dynasty: Della Torre family; Ruler title: Lord; First ruler: Martino della Torre; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Duchy of Milan

name: Federation of the Seven Communes
label: holy roman empire
description: The Federation of the Seven Communes was an autonomous highland peasant democracy established across the Asiago Plateau in the Venetian Prealps following the collapse of the Ezzelini tyranny. Comprising seven Cimbrian-speaking rural communities, the federation coordinated shared mountain pastures, timber exploitation and local defence through an elected central regent and communal council. The league successfully defended its ancient communal charters and fiscal exemptions for centuries before making a voluntary act of dedication to Venice. \n\n Status: Autonomous rural federation; Capital: Asiago; Common languages: Cimbrian and Venetian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Federal direct democracy; Ruler title: Regent; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Republic of Venice

name: Goryeo
description: Goryeo was a Korean kingdom that endured tributary subjugation under the Mongol Empire following decades of destructive continental warfare and military resistance. Operating from the fortified island redoubt of Ganghwa, the Korean monarchy surrendered after the military dictatorship was overthrown by peace advocates who dispatched the crown prince to negotiate with Kublai Khan. In 1260, the realm concluded a formal peace settlement, agreeing to provide tribute, grain supplies and auxiliary troops to the Great Khan while retaining its royal dynasty. \n\n Status: Mongol vassal state; Capital: Ganghwa; Common languages: Middle Korean and Classical Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Wang dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Preceded by: Goryeo (Independent)

name: Kingdom of Sicily (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of Sicily (Military Occupation) represented the extraterritorial naval and military operations deployed across the central Mediterranean and coastal fortresses by the Hohenstaufen and Sicilian fleets. Administered directly by crown admirals and military captains from mobile naval commands, these garrisons guarded critical maritime choke points, enforced blockade controls and coordinated tactical interventions across the Adriatic and Ionian seas. The occupation commands maintained strategic dominance until political realignments transformed Sicilian Mediterranean governance. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile operational command; Common languages: Sicilian, Latin and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military administration; Ruler title: Military Commander; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Sicily

name: Signoria of Camerino
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Camerino was an autonomous medieval state established in the central Apennines between the Potenza and Chienti river valleys in the Marche region. Governed by the noble Da Varano dynasty, the signoria held strategic dominance over vital trans-Apennine communication highways linking Umbria to the Adriatic coast. The Da Varano rulers fostered regional trade, patronised educational institutions such as the local university and maintained their domestic sovereignty through astute diplomatic manoeuvring between neighbouring popes and emperors. \n\n Status: Imperial signoria; Capital: Camerino; Common languages: Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Signorial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Da Varano family; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Historical region: Marche

name: Ariq Böke
label: successors of the mongol empire
description: Ariq Böke was a claimant state within the Mongol Empire established by Ariq Böke, a grandson of Genghis Khan, who was proclaimed Khagan at an assembly in Karakorum in 1260. Supported by conservative Mongol princes and nomadic traditionalists of the Mongolian heartland, his regime contested the imperial succession against his brother Kublai in the Toluid Civil War. Ariq Böke's government controlled the imperial capital and the ancestral Mongolian steppes until severe food blockades and military defeats forced his surrender in 1264. \n\n Status: Imperial claimant state; Capital: Karakorum; Common languages: Middle Mongol; Religion: Tengrism; Government: Steppe monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Borjigin dynasty; Ruler title: Khagan; First ruler: Ariq Böke; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Great Yuan

name: Chagatai Khanate
label: successors of the mongol empire
description: The Chagatai Khanate was an independent Mongol imperial realm that governed the Central Asian steppe and Transoxiana following the political fracturing of the unified Mongol Empire. Ruled by descendants of Chagatai Khan from their seasonal capitals in the Ili Valley, the nomadic empire controlled prosperous Silk Road oases including Bukhara and Samarkand. Although initially preserving Mongolian steppe customs, the ruling elite gradually embraced Turkic culture and Islam, maintaining regional hegemony until fragmenting into Moghulistan and the Timurid Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign khanate; Capital: Almaliq; Common languages: Middle Mongol and Chagatai Turkic; Religion: Tengrism and Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Genghisid dynasty; Ruler title: Khan; First ruler: Chagatai Khan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Mongol Empire

name: County of Tripoli
label: crusader states
description: The County of Tripoli was a Levantine Crusader state in northern Lebanon that operated as a tributary vassal under the Ilkhanate following the formal division of the Mongol Empire. Governed by Count Bohemond VI and his successors, the Frankish county relied on Mongol military protection against aggressive encirclement by the Mamluk Sultanate of Cairo. This geopolitical alignment failed to save the coastal state when Sultan Qalawun launched a massive siege that captured and dismantled the county in 1289. \n\n Status: Ilkhanate vassal state; Capital: Tripoli; Common languages: Old French, Latin and Arabic; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Poitiers-Antioch; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Mamluk Sultanate

name: Đại Việt
description: Đại Việt was a Vietnamese monarchy in the Red River delta that maintained formal tributary relations with the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty in China during the early 1260s. King Trần Thánh Tông engaged in delicate diplomatic negotiations, offering triennial tributary gifts to Dadu while steadfastly refusing Mongol demands for imperial tax inspectors and royal hostagetaking. This precarious tributary relationship soon collapsed into open warfare as Kublai Khan attempted direct military invasions of the kingdom, which were decisively repelled by Vietnamese armies. \n\n Status: Yuan tributary kingdom; Capital: Thang Long; Official languages: Literary Chinese; Common languages: Vietnamese; Religion: Mahayana Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Trần dynasty; Ruler title: King; First ruler: Trần Thánh Tông; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Preceded by: Đại Việt

name: Dali Kingdom
description: The Dali Kingdom existed as an autonomous tributary dependency under the Yuan dynasty of China following the pacification of south-western Yunnan. Governed by hereditary chieftains of the deposed Duan royal house serving as imperial tusi magistrates, the polity preserved traditional Bai administrative institutions, Buddhist monasteries and local customary laws. The Duan tusi managed regional tribal pacification and maintained caravan commerce with mainland Southeast Asia until the Ming conquest in 1382 fully annexed Yunnan. \n\n Status: Yuan vassal kingdom; Capital: Dali; Common languages: Bai and Literary Chinese; Religion: Buddhism; Government: Hereditary tusi monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Duan dynasty; Ruler title: Tusi; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Ming Dynasty

name: Empire of Trebizond
label: byzantine fragmentation
description: The Empire of Trebizond was a Pontic Greek Byzantine successor state on the southern Black Sea coast that continued as a tributary vassal under the Mongol Ilkhanate. Governed by the Megas Komnenos dynasty from the citadel of Trabzon, the empire paid annual gold tribute to the Ilkhan court at Tabriz in exchange for security against Seljuk and Turkmen raids. This vassalage protected the realm's lucrative transit trade along the northern terminus of the overland Silk Road, facilitating cultural and architectural patronisation. \n\n Status: Ilkhanate vassal empire; Capital: Trabzon; Common languages: Pontic Greek; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Megas Komnenos; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Empire of Trebizond

name: Golden Horde
label: successors of the mongol empire
description: The Golden Horde, officially known as the Ulus of Jochi, was an independent Mongol and Turkic khanate that dominated the vast Eurasian steppes from the Danube to western Siberia. Established by Batu Khan with its capital at Sarai on the lower Volga River, the empire exercised supreme tributary overlordship across the fragmented Rus' principalities. The horde grew exceptionally wealthy through the regulation of international Silk Road commerce, adopting Islam as its official state religion under Özbeg Khan before fracturing into regional khanates. \n\n Status: Sovereign nomadic empire; Capital: Sarai; Common languages: Kipchak Turkic and Middle Mongol; Religion: Tengrism and Sunni Islam; Government: Semi-elective monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jochid dynasty; Ruler title: Khan; First ruler: Batu Khan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Mongol Empire

name: Goryeo
description: Goryeo was a Korean kingdom that became a closely integrated tributary vassal under the Mongol Yuan dynasty after kingly authority was restored to Kaesong. Under this vassalage arrangement, Korean monarchs wedded imperial Yuan princesses, adopted Mongol administrative customs and supplied extensive naval resources for the Mongol invasions of Japan. Despite heavy political interference from imperial proconsuls, Goryeo maintained its distinct institutional continuity and bureaucratic examinations until King Gongmin reclaimed full independence in the mid-fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Yuan vassal kingdom; Capital: Kaesong; Common languages: Early Middle Korean and Classical Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Confucianism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Wang dynasty; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Goryeo

name: Grand Principality of Vladimir
label: russian principalities
description: The Grand Principality of Vladimir was the senior East Slavic principality of north-eastern Rus' that governed as a tributary vassal state under the Golden Horde following the division of the Mongol Empire. Grand princes such as Alexander Nevsky and his descendants secured yarlyk investiture patents from the khans at Sarai, which granted them authority to collect imperial taxes and arbitrate inter-princely disputes. This administrative hegemony preserved the Orthodox Church and gradually shifted regional political dominance towards the appanages of Moscow and Tver. \n\n Status: Golden Horde vassal state; Capital: Vladimir; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Ruler title: Grand Prince; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Grand Principality of Vladimir

name: Great Yuan
label: successors of the mongol empire
description: The Great Yuan was an imperial conquest dynasty founded by Kublai Khan that united the Mongol Empire's eastern realms with mainland China, governing from the new imperial metropolis of Dadu. Adopting traditional Chinese bureaucratic institutions and imperial regalia while preserving Mongol military hegemony, the dynasty established administrative provinces across China, Korea and the Mongolian homeland. The Yuan promoted international maritime trade, introduced paper currency systems and fostered cosmopolitan intellectual exchanges before peasant rebellions forced the imperial court to retreat northwards. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Beijing; Common languages: Middle Mongol and Old Mandarin; Religion: Buddhism, Confucianism and Tengrism; Government: Imperial monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Borjigin dynasty; Ruler title: Emperor; First ruler: Kublai Khan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Mongol Empire; Succeeded by: Ming Dynasty

name: Ilkhanate
label: successors of the mongol empire
description: The Ilkhanate was an independent Mongol realm established in south-western Asia by Hulegu Khan following the conquest of Baghdad and the collapse of the Abbasid Caliphate. Spanning modern Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan and eastern Anatolia, the state was administered from capitals at Maragheh and Tabriz, where the Mongol elite integrated into Persian administrative traditions. Following the conversion of Ghazan Khan to Islam in 1295, the Ilkhanate experienced an artistic and cultural golden age before succumbing to dynastic fragmentation and the Black Death. \n\n Status: Sovereign khanate; Capital: Maragheh; Common languages: Persian, Middle Mongol and Turkic; Religion: Mongolian Buddhism and Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Huleguid dynasty; Ruler title: Ilkhan; First ruler: Hulegu Khan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Mongol Empire

name: Kingdom of Eastern Georgia
description: The Kingdom of Eastern Georgia emerged as a regional feudal entity following the division of the realm during the period of Mongol dominance across the South Caucasus. Governed from Tbilisi under the sovereignty of David VII and his successors, the kingdom operated as a subordinate tributary of the Ilkhanate while western territories seceded under rival Bagrationi dynasts. Continued Mongol administrative interference and military levies constrained its authority until George V reunited the Georgian lands in the early fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Ilkhanate; Capital: Tbilisi; Common languages: Middle Georgian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Georgia; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Georgia

name: Kingdom of Imereti
description: The Kingdom of Imereti originated in western Georgia when David VI established an independent court away from Mongol hegemony, creating an autonomous bastion around the Rioni river basin. Centred on the royal stronghold of Kutaisi, the realm experienced recurring intervals of full independence punctuated by periodic reintegration into the broader Georgian kingdom. Its sovereign monarchs maintained western Georgian cultural institutions and defended mountain passes against surrounding regional powers. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kutaisi; Common languages: Georgian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bagrationi; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Georgia; Succeeded by: Russian Empire

name: Kingdom of Qocho
description: The Kingdom of Qocho, also known as the Idiqut state, functioned as a Buddhist Uyghur monarchy nestled in the fertile oases of the Turpan Depression. Following the partition of the broader Mongol realms, the idiquts maintained local administration as loyal tributaries beneath the suzerainty of the Chagatai Khanate. The kingdom sustained lively caravan commerce along northern Silk Road branches until political turbulence and Islamic conversion movements in the fourteenth century led to its complete absorption. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Chagatai Khanate; Capital: Qocho; Common languages: Old Uyghur and Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism and Church of the East; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Idiqut; Historical era: Middle Ages; Preceded by: Uyghur Khaganate; Succeeded by: Chagatai Khanate

name: Kingdom of Rus'
description: The Kingdom of Rus', historically rooted in the southwestern principality of Galicia-Volhynia, maintained a fragile autonomy under the overlordship of the Golden Horde. Having received a royal crown from the papacy in the mid-thirteenth century, its rulers established their administrative seat at Lviv and governed extensive territories spanning the Dniester and Bug basins. The kingdom preserved East Slavic Orthodox traditions and resisted steppe incursions until its ruling Rurikid line failed, prompting partition among neighbouring powers. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Golden Horde; Capital: Lviv; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Galicia-Volhynia; Succeeded by: Ruthenian Voivodeship

name: Kingdom of Western Georgia
description: The Kingdom of Western Georgia arose during the fragmentation of the medieval Georgian state as local rulers sought refuge beyond the Likhi Range from Mongol incursions. Operating with Kutaisi as its administrative capital, the realm accepted nominal vassalage under the Ilkhanate while maintaining substantial domestic autonomy over its western principalities. Internal factional strife among regional magnates gradually weakened royal control until central Georgian authority was restored in the 1330s. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Ilkhanate; Capital: Kutaisi; Common languages: Middle Georgian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Georgia; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Georgia

name: Lord Novgorod the Great
label: russian principalities
description: Lord Novgorod the Great was a prosperous medieval merchant republic that dominated vast boreal expanses from the Baltic Sea to the Ural Mountains. Although the city preserved unique communal institutions governed by an elected veche and a merchant patriciate, it acknowledged formal subordination and dispatched tribute to the Golden Horde. Its lucrative commerce through the Hanseatic network supported a vibrant artistic culture until the territorial ambitions of Moscow extinguished its municipal liberties in 1478. \n\n Status: Republican vassal of the Golden Horde; Capital: Veliky Novgorod; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Merchant republic; Legislature: Veche; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Principality of Antioch
description: The Principality of Antioch was one of the original crusader realms in the Levant, established along the Orontes river valley during the First Crusade. Facing severe encirclement by the ascendant Mamluk Sultanate, Prince Bohemond VI aligned the enclave as a tributary of the Mongol Ilkhanate to safeguard its remaining coastal and northern Syrian territories. This Mongol alliance failed to prevent the siege and decisive sack of Antioch by Sultan Baibars in June 1268, which permanently eliminated the principality. \n\n Status: Tributary principality of the Ilkhanate; Capital: Antioch; Common languages: Old French, Medieval Latin and Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruler title: Prince of Antioch; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Mamluk Sultanate

name: Principality of Chernigov
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Chernigov was an ancient East Slavic domain situated across the Desna river basin in modern northern Ukraine and neighbouring Russian borderlands. Devastated by the thirteenth-century Mongol invasion, the principality survived under the dynastic rule of the Olgovichi as a subordinate client paying tribute to the Golden Horde. Ongoing territorial splintering and depopulation ultimately weakened the polity, allowing the Grand Duchy of Lithuania to incorporate its core lands during the fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of the Golden Horde; Capital: Chernihiv; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Olgovichi; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

name: Principality of Kiev
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Kiev retained profound symbolic prestige as the cradle of Rus' civilisation, despite enduring immense destruction and demographic decline following the Mongol sack of 1240. Operating within a restricted territorial footprint around the middle Dnieper, its rulers held the grand princely patent under strict supervision and fiscal exploitation from the Golden Horde. The enfeebled principality maintained fragile urban life and monastic centres until expanding Lithuanian forces absorbed the region in the 1320s. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of the Golden Horde; Capital: Kyiv; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Grand Prince; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

name: Principality of Pereyaslavl
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Pereyaslavl occupied a vital southern march of historical Rus', protecting riverine trade routes along the Trubizh and Dnieper rivers. Heavily battered by nomadic raids and subsequent Mongol conquests, the realm functioned as a diminished dependency under the direct overrule of the Golden Horde throughout the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Its princes retained limited local authority over fortified settlements until the principality was definitively absorbed by the Lithuanian realm. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of the Golden Horde; Capital: Pereiaslav; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

name: Principality of Pereyaslavl-Zalessky
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Pereyaslavl-Zalessky was an influential northeastern Rus' appanage centred on Lake Pleshcheyevo in the historic Zalesye region. Ruled by cadet members of the Vladimir-Suzdal ducal house, the principality paid tribute to the Golden Horde and frequently served as a key base for prominent princes including Alexander Nevsky. Upon the death of Prince Ivan Dmitrievich without direct heirs in 1302, the territory was bequeathed to Daniel of Moscow, initiating its permanent integration into the nascent Muscovite state. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of the Golden Horde; Capital: Pereslavl-Zalessky; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Vladimir-Suzdal; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Principality of Rostov
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Rostov was a prominent north-Russian realm clustered around Lake Nero, renowned for its ancient episcopal seat and strong merchant traditions. Subordinated as a tributary appanage under the khans of the Golden Horde, the principality suffered from repeated internal divisions among rival princely branches. Although local rulers retained formal administrative prerogatives throughout the fourteenth century, persistent financial dependency enabled the Grand Duchy of Moscow to buy up shares and eventually annex the territory in 1474. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of the Golden Horde; Capital: Rostov; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Vladimir-Suzdal; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Principality of Ryazan
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Ryazan held a strategic and exposed position along the Oka river valley, directly confronting the southern steppe frontier. After the cataclysmic destruction of Old Ryazan by Batu Khan, the capital was re-established at Pereyaslavl-Ryazansky under the tributary oversight of the Golden Horde. The resilient principality managed to preserve diplomatic leeway and military autonomy against both Mongol incursions and Muscovite expansion before gradually succumbing to Moscow's political hegemony in the late fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of the Golden Horde; Capital: Ryazan; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Principality of Murom-Ryazan; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Principality of Smolensk
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Smolensk commanded crucial overland portages and waterways linking the upper Dnieper with the Baltic and Volga basins. Under the tributary framework imposed by the Golden Horde, the local dynasty governed an extensive territory that functioned as a vital commercial hub between northern Rus' and central Europe. Internal succession rivalries and increasing pressure from neighbouring powers weakened the realm, facilitating its gradual incorporation into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania towards the turn of the fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of the Golden Horde; Capital: Smolensk; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kievan Rus'; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

name: Principality of Turov
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Turov encompassed the swampy woodlands and river valleys of the Pripyat Marshes in present-day southern Belarus and northern Ukraine. Operating under the suzerainty of the Golden Horde following the Mongol onslaught, the principality experienced marked decentralisation, fracturing into smaller patrimonies such as Pinsk and Slutsk. Its rulers maintained traditional Slavic ecclesiastical customs until the expanding Lithuanian grand dukes absorbed the Polesian territories during the first half of the fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of the Golden Horde; Capital: Turov; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

name: Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia
description: The Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia flourished along the eastern Mediterranean coast and Taurus Mountains as a distinct Armenian sovereign realm established by refugees fleeing Seljuk conquests. Entering into a formal tributary alliance with the Mongol Ilkhanate under King Hethum I, the monarchy secured temporary military protection against neighbouring Muslim sultanates while serving as an indispensable partner for European crusaders. Sis remained its bustling ecclesiastical and administrative centre until continuous Mamluk offensives gradually undermined the state. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Ilkhanate; Capital: Sis; Common languages: Middle Armenian and Old French; Religion: Armenian Apostolic Christianity; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hethumid; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Mamluk Sultanate

name: Sultanate of Rum
description: The Sultanate of Rum was a Turco-Persian Islamic monarchy that reshaped medieval Anatolia following the eleventh-century Seljuk advance. Severely defeated at the Battle of Kose Dag, the sultanate was reduced to an Ilkhanid client state administered from its ornate capital at Konya under heavy Mongol fiscal exactions. Although royal institutions and cultural patronages lingered, imperial authority disintegrated rapidly, giving rise to numerous autonomous Turkmen beyliks across western and central Anatolia. \n\n Status: Vassal sultanate of the Ilkhanate; Capital: Konya; Common languages: Persian, Old Anatolian Turkish and Byzantine Greek; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic sultanate; Ruling dynasty: Seljuk; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Anatolian beyliks

name: Duchy of Athens
label: frankokratia
description: The Duchy of Athens was established in the wake of the Fourth Crusade, encompassing the historical territories of Attica and Boeotia under western European feudal customs. Following the reconquest of Constantinople by the Byzantines in 1261, the duchy enjoyed an interval of direct sovereign autonomy under the French de la Roche dynasty. Governed between the acropolis at Athens and the prosperous commercial town of Thebes, the principality successfully maintained western chivalric institutions while managing an Orthodox Greek populace. \n\n Status: Sovereign crusader duchy; Capital: Athens; Common languages: Old French and Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Duke of Athens; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Latin Empire; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Grand Duchy of Lemnos
label: frankokratia
description: The Grand Duchy of Lemnos was an insular crusader lordship situated in the northern Aegean Sea, originally awarded to the Venetian-Frankish Navigajoso family as a fief of the Latin Empire. When Constantinople fell to the Palaiologan Byzantines in 1261, the dynasts on Lemnos maintained autonomous control over the island from the formidable fortress of Myrina. The maritime principality guarded regional trade routes until the Byzantine fleet under Licario conquered the stronghold in 1279. \n\n Status: Sovereign island duchy; Capital: Myrina; Common languages: Old French, Italian and Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Preceded by: Latin Empire; Succeeded by: Byzantine Empire

name: Lordship of Salona
label: frankokratia
description: The Lordship of Salona was founded in central Greece during the division of Byzantine lands following the Fourth Crusade, taking its name from the ancient acropolis of Amphissa. Operating with sovereign independence after the collapse of the Latin Empire in 1261, the d'Autremencourt lords controlled pivotal routes between the Gulf of Corinth and the Boeotian plains. The well-fortified barony repelled neighbouring Greek and Frankish incursions until later regional upheavals brought Catalan and Navarrese rulers into power. \n\n Status: Sovereign crusader lordship; Capital: Salona; Common languages: Old French and Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruler title: Lord of Salona; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Marquisate of Bodonitsa
label: frankokratia
description: The Marquisate of Bodonitsa was established in eastern central Greece to guard the vital strategic pass of Thermopylae against hostile incursions. After shedding its nominal subordination to the Latin Empire, the margravial seat at Bodonitsa functioned as a resilient sovereign redoubt governed by the Pallavicini and later the Venetian Zorzi families. The enclave outlasted the arrival of the Catalan Company and numerous regional upheavals before finally succumbing to Ottoman conquest in 1414. \n\n Status: Sovereign margraviate; Capital: Bodonitsa; Common languages: Old French, Italian and Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Margrave; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Principality of Achaea
label: frankokratia
description: The Principality of Achaea, often termed the Principality of the Morea, formed the foremost crusader state in southern Greece following the Frankish partition of the Byzantine Empire. Following the fall of the Latin Empire in 1261, Prince William II of Villehardouin ruled the Peloponnese with complete autonomy from his court at Andravida. Achaea cultivated a vibrant chivalric culture and complex feudal law code, though recurrent border warfare with the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea gradually eroded its territorial reach. \n\n Status: Sovereign crusader principality; Capital: Andravida; Common languages: Old French and Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Villehardouin; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Despotate of the Morea

name: Beylik of Lâdik
label: anatolian beyliks
description: The Beylik of Lâdik, ruled by the Inanjid dynasty, was an autonomous Turkmen frontier principality established around the ancient city of Laodicea on the Lycus, modern Denizli. Emerging amidst the gradual contraction of the Sultanate of Rum, the beylik defended western Anatolian mountain passes and conducted profitable trade along inland river routes. Its rulers maintained diplomatic flexibility between rival Anatolian neighbours until the expanding Ottoman state ultimately incorporated the territory in the late fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Denizli; Common languages: Old Anatolian Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Inanjids; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Sultanate of Rum; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: County of Holstein-Itzehoe
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Holstein-Itzehoe was a northern German imperial principality created in 1261 through the partition of the County of Holstein between the brothers Gerhard I and John I. Governed by Count Gerhard from his fortified administrative seat at Itzehoe, the state exerted control over fertile marshlands between the Stör and Elbe rivers. Gerhard vigorously expanded dynastic power and promoted urban trade until his death in 1290, after which the county was subdivided among his three surviving sons. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Itzehoe; Common languages: Middle Low German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Schauenburg; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Preceded by: County of Holstein; Succeeded by: County of Holstein-Rendsburg

name: County of Holstein-Kiel
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Holstein-Kiel came into being in 1261 when the Schauenburg lands in Holstein were formally apportioned among family claimants, assigning the Baltic maritime districts to Count John I. Operating from the port town of Kiel, the counts fostered maritime commerce, granted lucrative civic privileges and engaged in regional Baltic diplomacy. The county remained an autonomous member of the Holy Roman Empire for over a century until dynastic extinction in 1390 led to its integration into Holstein-Rendsburg. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Kiel; Common languages: Middle Low German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Schauenburg; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: County of Holstein; Succeeded by: County of Holstein-Rendsburg

name: Greenland
label: norse/viking polities
description: Greenland became an overseas possession of the Norwegian crown in 1261 after the Norse colonists of the Eastern and Western Settlements agreed to submit to King Haakon IV. Administered spiritually from the episcopal seat at Gardar, the island community relied on the annual royal trading vessel to export walrus ivory and falcons in exchange for timber and iron. Climatic deterioration, shifting European commerce and increasing isolation gradually led to the abandonment of the Norse colonies during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. \n\n Status: Norwegian crown possession; Capital: Gardar; Common languages: Old Norse; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Overseas colonial dependency; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Denmark-Norway

name: Despotate of the Morea
label: frankokratia
description: The Despotate of the Morea was a flourishing semi-autonomous province of the Byzantine Empire governed by imperial dynasts from the Palaiologos and Kantakouzenos families. Centred on the fortified hillside capital of Mystras in the Peloponnese, the despotate became a renowned hearth of the late Byzantine cultural renaissance and classical philosophy. Its rulers steadily reclaimed territories from surrounding Frankish principalities, maintaining defensive autonomy until Ottoman armies conquered the peninsula in the aftermath of Constantinople's fall. \n\n Status: Semi-autonomous appanage of the Byzantine Empire; Capital: Mystras; Common languages: Medieval Greek; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Appanage principality; Ruler title: Despot of the Morea; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Dharampur State
description: Dharampur State was an autonomous Rajput principality established in 1262 across the rugged hills and forests of the southern Gujarat region. Founded by Ramshah of the Sisodia dynasty, the ruling house governed from the capital of Dharampur, maintaining sovereignty through agile diplomacy and tactical defence in the Western Ghats. The state preserved its local autonomy against surrounding regional powers for centuries before eventually coming under Maratha influence and later British paramountcy. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Dharampur; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sisodia Rajput; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: British East India Company

name: Free Imperial City of Strasbourg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Strasbourg achieved autonomy from the Prince-Bishop of Strasbourg in 1262 following the burghers' victory at the Battle of Hausbergen. Located on the left bank of the Rhine in Alsace, the self-governing city flourished as a pivotal commercial crossroads and cultural centre renowned for its soaring cathedral. Strasbourg embraced the Protestant Reformation in the sixteenth century and maintained its imperial freedom until King Louis XIV incorporated it into France in 1681. \n\n Status: Free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Strasbourg; Common languages: Alemannic German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Urban republic; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France

name: Salghurids
description: The Salghurids, widely known as the Atabegs of Fars, were a Persianate dynasty of Salur Turkoman lineage who held sway over southwestern Iran. Following the Mongol subjugation of the region, the atabegs governed Shiraz as obedient vassals of the Ilkhanate, remitting revenue while cultivating artistic and literary pursuits at court. Female ruler Abish Khatun reigned during the dynasty's final decades until direct Ilkhanid administration displaced the Salghurid house entirely in the 1280s. \n\n Status: Vassal atabegate of the Ilkhanate; Capital: Shiraz; Common languages: Persian and Turkic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Atabeg; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Seljuk Empire; Succeeded by: Ilkhanate

name: Signoria of Verona
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Verona was a powerful north Italian city-state governed by the della Scala dynasty from the mid-thirteenth century onward. Under ambitious leaders like Cangrande I, the Scaliger lordship expanded across the Veneto, transforming Verona into a fortified centre of arts, civic architecture and Ghibelline politics. The signoria maintained its sovereign stature in regional Italian conflicts until domestic rivalries weakened the regime, culminating in its annexation by the Republic of Venice in the early fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign signoria; Capital: Verona; Common languages: Venetian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Princely signoria; Ruling dynasty: Della Scala; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Republic of Venice

name: Grand Duchy of Lithuania
description: The Grand Duchy of Lithuania consolidated as a major northeastern European power following the murder of King Mindaugas, reverting to indigenous pagan leadership while resisting aggressive Teutonic crusades. Governed successively from Kernave, Trakai and ultimately Vilnius, the grand duchy rapidly expanded south and east into the fragmented lands of former Kievan Rus'. Through skilled diplomacy and military prowess against both crusading knights and Mongol armies, Lithuania established an enormous multi-ethnic and multi-confessional realm. \n\n Status: Sovereign grand duchy; Capital: Vilnius; Common languages: Lithuanian and Ruthenian; Religion: Baltic paganism, Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Grand Duke; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Polish-Lithuanian Union

name: Grand Duchy of Moscow
description: The Grand Duchy of Moscow originated in 1263 as a modest appanage awarded to Daniel, the youngest son of Alexander Nevsky, within the broader Vladimir-Suzdal lands. Subject to the overlordship of the Golden Horde, the Muscovite princes skilfully collected Mongol tributes, expanded their territory and secured the seat of the Russian Orthodox metropolitanate. Moscow steadily centralised power among northeastern Russian principalities until the Great Stand on the Ugra River in 1480 terminated two centuries of Mongol suzerainty. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of the Golden Horde; Capital: Moscow; Common languages: Russian and Church Slavonic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurikid; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Tsardom of Russia

name: Landgraviate of Hesse
label: holy roman empire
description: The Landgraviate of Hesse was an imperial principality founded in 1264 by Henry I following the War of the Thuringian Succession, separating Hessian territories from Thuringia. Governed primarily from Kassel and Marburg, the landgraviate expanded through careful territorial acquisitions and consolidated judicial authority within the Holy Roman Empire. The state emerged as an influential champion of the Protestant Reformation under Landgrave Philip the Magnanimous before his death in 1567 prompted a dynastic partition among his four sons. \n\n Status: Imperial principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Kassel; Common languages: German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Landgrave; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Landgraviate of Hesse-Kassel

name: Principality of Gorodets
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Gorodets emerged along the upper Volga river as an autonomous appanage carved out of the grand principality of Vladimir-Suzdal. Established around the fortified trading post of Gorodets, the realm was first ruled by Prince Andrey Alexandrovich, who utilised its strategic riverine location to project influence across eastern Rus'. The principality played a prominent role in regional succession struggles until its eventual absorption into the Principality of Nizhny Novgorod-Suzdal in the early fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Gorodets; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurikid; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Vladimir-Suzdal; Succeeded by: Principality of Nizhny Novgorod-Suzdal

name: Kingdom of Makuria
label: christian kingdoms of nubia
description: The Kingdom of Makuria was a Christian Nubian state that occupied the Middle Nile between the third and fourth cataracts. In 1265, invading Mamluk forces compelled the court at Dongola to submit to Cairo's suzerainty, inaugurating recurring periods of vassalage marked by forced tribute payments and rival pretenders. Despite repeated military interventions and growing internal instability, Makuria preserved its distinct Nubian Christian ecclesiastical hierarchy and ceremonial traditions into the fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Mamluk Sultanate; Capital: Dongola; Common languages: Old Nubian and Arabic; Religion: Coptic Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Banu Kanz

name: Kingdom of Mangyül Gungthang
description: The Kingdom of Mangyül Gungthang was established in southwestern Tibet around 1265 by Bumdegon, a descendant of the ancient Tibetan imperial dynasty. Headquartered at the fortified citadel of Dzongkar, the realm controlled critical trans-Himalayan trade routes linking the Tibetan plateau with Nepal. Although nominally associated with the Sakya administrative system, the kingdom maintained independent domestic governance and sponsored prestigious Buddhist scholastic establishments until it was conquered by the King of Tsang in 1620. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Dzongkar; Common languages: Classical Tibetan; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bumdegon; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Tsangpa dynasty

name: Marquisate of Olivola
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Olivola was a compact feudal state situated in the rugged Lunigiana region of modern northwestern Tuscany. Originating from a dynastic division of the Malaspina family estates in the thirteenth century, the marquisate was administered from the fortified village of Olivola near Aulla. The local margraves jealously guarded their imperial immediacy and feudal tolls along mountain transit passes until dynastic sales and regional reorganisations transferred the territory to Florence in 1569. \n\n Status: Imperial fief of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Aulla; Common languages: Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal marquisate; Ruling dynasty: Malaspina; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Tuscany

name: Kingdom of Sicily
description: The Kingdom of Sicily was captured by Charles I of Anjou in 1266 following his decisive victory over Manfred of Hohenstaufen at the Battle of Benevento. Charles governed both the island of Sicily and the southern Italian mainland, imposing centralised Angevin administration and heavy taxation to fund his Mediterranean ambitions. Angevin rule on the island collapsed abruptly during the popular uprising known as the Sicilian Vespers in 1282, which ultimately split the kingdom into two rival crowns. \n\n Status: Sovereign monarchy; Capital: Palermo and Naples; Common languages: Sicilian, Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Anjou; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Naples

name: Samtskhe-Saatabago
description: Samtskhe-Saatabago, also known as the Principality of Samtskhe, was an autonomous feudal state in southern Georgia ruled by the powerful Jaqeli dynasty. Centred at the mountain fortress of Akhaltsikhe, the principality covered the historic regions of Meskheti and Tao-Klarjeti.
