Following disputes with the central royal court in the late thirteenth century, the atabegs asserted de facto independence, preserving distinctive Georgian Christian culture and military traditions until expanding Ottoman armies subjugated the region. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Akhaltsikhe; Common languages: Georgian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: Jaqeli; Ruler title: Atabeg of Samtskhe; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Childir Eyalet

name: Duchy of Athens
label: frankokratia
description: The Duchy of Athens became a feudal dependency of Charles I of Anjou through the Treaty of Viterbo in 1267, subordinating the crusader realm to the Angevin Kingdom of Sicily. Governed locally by the French de la Roche dukes from Athens and Thebes, the duchy provided military levies and diplomatic support for Angevin campaigns across Greece. Despite distant royal oversight, the local administration preserved its Frankish legal traditions and knightly assemblies throughout the late thirteenth century. \n\n Status: Vassal duchy of the Kingdom of Sicily; Capital: Athens; Common languages: Old French and Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Duke of Athens; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Crown of Aragon

name: Lordship of Salona
label: frankokratia
description: The Lordship of Salona entered into vassalage under Charles I of Anjou following the diplomatic accords signed at Viterbo in 1267. Situated around the formidable mountain fortress of Amphissa in central Greece, the d'Autremencourt barony maintained local governance while swearing feudal fealty to the Angevin monarchy in Naples. The lords contributed troops to Angevin defensive initiatives across the Morea until the cataclysmic Catalan conquest of the region in the early fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Vassal lordship of the Kingdom of Sicily; Capital: Amphissa; Common languages: Old French and Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruler title: Lord of Salona; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Catalan Company

name: Principality of Achaea
label: frankokratia
description: The Principality of Achaea became a direct vassal state of the Angevin crown in 1267 when Prince William II surrendered sovereignty to Charles I of Anjou under the Treaty of Viterbo. Administered through royal seneschals from Andravida, the Morean baronies received substantial Neapolitan military and financial reinforcements to repel Byzantine counter-offensives. This feudal arrangement protected Frankish strongholds in the Peloponnese until dynastic inheritance returned the principality to direct Villehardouin descendancy in 1289. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of the Kingdom of Sicily; Capital: Andravida; Common languages: Old French and Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Anjou; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Principality of Achaea

name: Samudera Pasai Sultanate
description: The Samudera Pasai Sultanate was an influential maritime Islamic kingdom established on the northern coast of Sumatra around 1267 by Merah Silu, who assumed the regnal name Malik ul Salih. Positioned advantageously along the Strait of Malacca, the sultanate grew into a prosperous entrepot for international spices, textiles and religious scholarship. Pasai served as the primary springboard for the propagation of Islam throughout the Malay Archipelago before being absorbed by the neighbouring Sultanate of Aceh. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Pasai; Common languages: Old Malay and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early Modern; Preceded by: Peureulak Sultanate; Succeeded by: Aceh Sultanate

name: Sultanate of Kelantan
description: The Sultanate of Kelantan was an autonomous Malay realm established along the northeastern coastal plains of the Malay Peninsula. Anchored around the fertile delta of the Kelantan River, the monarchy maintained vibrant maritime trade relations with regional kingdoms and Chinese merchants. Its Muslim sovereigns governed as independent rulers during this period, preserving indigenous Malay customs and defending their territory against expansionist neighbouring empires. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Kota Bharu; Common languages: Classical Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Malacca Sultanate

name: Free Imperial City of Rottweil
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Rottweil acquired imperial immediacy in 1268, achieving complete autonomy within the Holy Roman Empire between the Black Forest and the Swabian Alps. Governed by a patrician municipal council, the town held prestigious regional jurisdiction as the seat of an imperial court of justice. Rottweil flourished through thriving grain and cattle markets along the upper Neckar, eventually entering into close defensive alliances with the Swiss cantons. \n\n Status: Free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Rottweil; Common languages: Swabian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Urban republic; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Duchy of Swabia; Succeeded by: Swiss Confederation

name: Free Imperial City of Überlingen
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Überlingen attained independent imperial status in 1268, emerging as an autonomous civic republic on the northern shore of Lake Constance. Its municipal senate oversaw expanding lake commerce, renowned viticulture and extensive regional grain distribution networks. Endowed with formidable ramparts and stone bastions, the city steadfastly defended its imperial privileges against surrounding dynastic lords until the territorial mediatisation of the early nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Überlingen; Common languages: Alemannic German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Urban republic; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Margraviate of Baden

name: Principality of Great Wallachia
description: The Principality of Great Wallachia was an autonomous medieval state established across the plains and mountain highlands of Thessaly by John I Doukas after detaching from the Despotate of Epirus. Named after its substantial Aromanian and Vlach pastoral populations, the realm was governed from the citadel of Neopatras, modern Ypati. John I successfully repulsed Byzantine military campaigns and balanced alliances with Frankish crusader neighbours until internal fragmentation enabled the Catalan Company to overrun the territory. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Ypati; Common languages: Aromanian and Medieval Greek; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Sebastokrator; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Despotate of Epirus; Succeeded by: Catalan Company

name: Ethiopian Empire
description: The Ethiopian Empire was inaugurated around 1270 when Yekuno Amlak overthrew the Zagwe dynasty, establishing the Solomonic dynasty and claiming direct lineage from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. Centred across the Ethiopian Highlands, the imperial monarchy initially maintained a mobile court of royal encampments before establishing fixed administrative seats at Gondar and later Addis Ababa. The Christian highland empire repelled external invasions for centuries, expanding southward and remaining an uncolonised sovereign bulwark in the Horn of Africa. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Gondar and Addis Ababa; Common languages: Amharic and Ge'ez; Religion: Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Solomonic; Ruler title: Emperor; Historical era: Middle Ages to Modern; Preceded by: Zagwe dynasty

name: Principality of Myshegda
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Myshegda was a small appanage state that arose among the Upper Oka Principalities in central Russia during the fragmentation of the Chernigov realm. Governed by a cadet Rurikid lineage from fortified strongpoints near the confluence of the Myshega and Oka rivers, the principality exercised local autonomy over forest and agricultural tracts. Its rulers navigated fluid alliances between rival Slavic dynasties and steppe overlords until the territory was absorbed into Muscovite lands during the fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Aleksin; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurikid; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Principality of Obolensk
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Obolensk emerged in the late thirteenth century along the right bank of the Protva River as a sovereign appanage of the Chernigov princely house. Founding a dynastic line known as the Obolensky princes, its rulers held judicial and territorial authority over fortified settlements in the central Russian woodlands. Positioned between expanding Muscovite and Lithuanian spheres, the small principality maintained sovereign independence for nearly a century before being formally integrated into the Grand Principality of Moscow. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Obolensk; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurikid; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Commune of Modigliana
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Modigliana emerged as an autonomous city-state in the Apennine foothills of the historic Romagna region, situated along the valley of the Tramigna. Having loosened the feudal dominion of the powerful Guidi counts in the late thirteenth century, the town established republican civic magistrates and codified municipal statutes. The commune defended its upland territory and commercial routes against surrounding Romagnol and Tuscan despots until expanding Florentine power eventually brought the municipality under Tuscan control. \n\n Status: Free medieval commune; Capital: Modigliana; Common languages: Romagnol and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Communal republic; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: County of the Guidi; Succeeded by: Republic of Florence

name: Sicilian Dependencies in Albania
description: The Sicilian Dependencies in Albania encompassed the Adriatic coastal strip and maritime fortresses captured by Charles I of Anjou from the Byzantine Empire in 1271. Administered by Angevin military captains headquartered at Durazzo, these holdings were held in personal union with the Sicilian crown as a strategic bridgehead for projected Balkan expansion. This brief interim administration concluded in late February 1272 when Charles formally proclaimed the creation of the Kingdom of Albania with the consent of local noblemen. \n\n Status: Coastal dependency of the Kingdom of Sicily; Capital: Durazzo; Common languages: Medieval Latin, Italian and Albanian; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Military administration; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Albania

name: Kingdom of Albania
description: The Kingdom of Albania was formally established on 21 February 1272 when Charles I of Anjou proclaimed himself king with the backing of local Albanian archons. Governed in personal union from the royal court at Naples, the kingdom stretched from the fortified port of Durazzo southward to the coastal haven of Butrint. Angevin garrisons defended these Adriatic outposts against determined Byzantine counter-attacks, preserving a crucial Mediterranean foothold until the indigenous Thopia dynasty seized Durazzo in 1368. \n\n Status: Monarchy in personal union with the Kingdom of Sicily; Capital: Durazzo; Common languages: Medieval Latin, Italian and Albanian; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Anjou; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Principality of Albania

name: Imperial City of Badenweiler
label: holy roman empire
description: The Imperial City of Badenweiler functioned as a self-governing imperial community in the Markgräflerland, situated at the western slopes of the Black Forest. Sheltered beneath the Blauen mountain, the town enjoyed autonomous legal rights within the Holy Roman Empire and prospered from its historic thermal springs and viticulture. Its civic authorities governed local administration and municipal courts until political pressures and territorial realignments in the fifteenth century led to its incorporation into the Margraviate of Baden. \n\n Status: Free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Badenweiler; Common languages: High Alemannic German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Urban council; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Duchy of Swabia; Succeeded by: Margraviate of Baden

name: Chiefdom of Sizhou
label: four great native chiefdoms in guizhou
description: The Chiefdom of Sizhou was a powerful hereditary tusi polity ruled by the Tian clan across the mountainous river valleys of eastern Guizhou. Subordinated to the Yuan and later Ming imperial courts as an autonomous frontier vassal, the chieftaincy governed diverse Tujia and Hmong populations under indigenous customary law. Regarded as one of the four great chiefdoms of Guizhou, Sizhou maintained substantial military autonomy until violent clan conflicts prompted the Ming court to annex the domain in 1413. \n\n Status: Autonomous native chiefdom of the Chinese Empire; Capital: Sizhou; Common languages: Tujia, Chinese and Hmong; Religion: Nuoism and Confucianism; Government: Hereditary chieftaincy; Ruling dynasty: Tian clan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Ming dynasty

name: County of Holstein-Segeberg
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Holstein-Segeberg was a temporary northern German principality established in 1273 for Count Adolphus V, nicknamed the Pomeranian, as an appanage carved from Holstein-Kiel. Centred upon the towering Kalkberg rock and its formidable castle at Bad Segeberg, the county governed surrounding rural districts and protected crucial overland routes between the Elbe and Baltic waters. Following the death of Adolphus V without heirs in 1308, the autonomous county was permanently reabsorbed into the County of Holstein-Kiel. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Bad Segeberg; Common languages: Middle Low German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Schauenburg; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: County of Holstein-Kiel; Succeeded by: County of Holstein-Kiel

name: County of Limpurg
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Limpurg was an imperial fief in northeastern Swabia held by the noble Schenken von Limpurg, who served as hereditary cupbearers of the Holy Roman Empire. Centred at Limpurg Castle and later from the residence at Gaildorf, the counts exercised immediate territorial sovereignty across the Kocher valley. The dynasty actively patronised regional commerce and embraced the Protestant Reformation before the extinction of the male line led to partition and eventual mediatisation into the Kingdom of Württemberg. \n\n Status: Imperial county of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Gaildorf; Common languages: Swabian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Limpurg; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Württemberg

name: County of Oettingen
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Oettingen was an imperial state of the Holy Roman Empire located in the fertile Nördlinger Ries basin between Swabia and Franconia. Governed by the high-ranking noble House of Oettingen from their ancestral seat at Oettingen in Bayern, the dynasty maintained immediate imperial status and held extensive rural manors. Despite frequent internal partitions into distinct lines, the counts retained their sovereign authority until their lands were elevated to principalities and subsequently incorporated into Bavaria in 1806. \n\n Status: Imperial county of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Oettingen in Bayern; Common languages: Swabian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Oettingen; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Bavaria

name: Domain of Braničevo
description: The Domain of Braničevo was an autonomous principality in modern eastern Serbia ruled jointly by the Bulgarian-Cuman boyar brothers Darman and Kudelin. Taking advantage of administrative decentralisation in Hungary and the Second Bulgarian Empire, the brothers operated from their formidable river citadel of Ždrelo on the Mlava. Relying on formidable Cuman and Tatar cavalry auxiliaries, they repelled Hungarian incursions and raided adjacent territories until King Stefan Dragutin and King Stefan Milutin combined forces to conquer the domain in the 1290s. \n\n Status: Sovereign autocracy; Capital: Braničevo; Common languages: Old Bulgarian and Cuman; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Dual rulership; Ruling dynasty: Darman and Kudelin; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Syrmia

name: Free Imperial City of Schwäbisch Gmünd
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Schwäbisch Gmünd was an autonomous urban republic situated in the Rems river valley in eastern Swabia. Securing imperial immediacy under the Staufer monarchs in the thirteenth century, the city developed a robust guild-based municipal council that oversaw lucrative goldsmithing, jewellery manufacture and regional commerce. Gmünd maintained its Catholic religious allegiance throughout the Reformation and fiercely defended its imperial independence until its annexation by the Duchy of Württemberg during the Napoleonic mediatisations. \n\n Status: Free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Schwäbisch Gmünd; Common languages: Swabian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Urban republic; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Württemberg

name: County of Santa Fiora
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Santa Fiora was formed in southern Tuscany in 1274 upon the partition of the extensive feudal estates of the Aldobrandeschi family. Administered from its fortified mountain capital at Santa Fiora on the slopes of Monte Amiata, the county exercised sovereign jurisdiction over key parts of the Maremma and southern Tuscan woodlands. Despite recurring conflicts with the Republic of Siena that sheared away outlying castellanies, Santa Fiora retained sovereign autonomy through marriage into the Sforza house. \n\n Status: Imperial county of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Santa Fiora; Common languages: Tuscan and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Aldobrandeschi and Sforza; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Tuscany

name: County of Sovana
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Sovana was established in central Italy in 1274 as the southern counterpart created by the division of the Aldobrandeschi dynastic patrimony. Governed from the ancient tuff-cliff fortress of Sovana, the county encompassed strategic territories across the upper Maremma and lower Fiora valley. The Aldobrandeschi rulers struggled against the persistent expansionist campaigns of the Republic of Siena, which steadily captured the county's strongholds until the polity was entirely annexed into the Sienese dominion in the 1330s. \n\n Status: Imperial county of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Sovana; Common languages: Tuscan and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Aldobrandeschi; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Republic of Siena

name: Free Imperial City of Rothenburg ob der Tauber
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Rothenburg ob der Tauber gained imperial immediacy in 1274 through a charter granted by King Rudolf I of Habsburg. Overlooking the scenic Tauber River in Middle Franconia, the city expanded behind formidable curtain walls and towers, developing into an influential commercial republic with extensive rural lands. Rothenburg maintained self-governing civic liberties and adopted the Lutheran confession during the Reformation, retaining its imperial autonomy until mediatised into the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1803. \n\n Status: Free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Rothenburg ob der Tauber; Common languages: East Franconian German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Urban republic; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Bavaria

name: Imperial Bailiwick of Lower Alsace
label: holy roman empire
description: The Imperial Bailiwick of Lower Alsace, known as the Landvogtei of Lower Alsace, was an administrative and judicial district of the Holy Roman Empire centred at Haguenau. Established to coordinate imperial peacekeeping and protect immediate estates across northern Alsace, the bailiwick encompassed numerous autonomous knightly fiefs, monastic domains and fledgling imperial towns. The imperial bailiff represented the crown's direct authority in the region until these collective urban communities consolidated into the defensive alliance of the Décapole. \n\n Status: Imperial bailiwick of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Haguenau; Common languages: Alemannic German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Imperial administration; Ruler title: Landvogt; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Décapole

name: Free Imperial City of Buchhorn
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Buchhorn attained imperial immediacy in 1275, establishing an independent urban administration on the northern shore of Lake Constance. Centred at the historic port settlement that later became Friedrichshafen, the small city thrived as a transport hub for timber, grain and regional goods ferried across the alpine lake. Its municipal council maintained sovereign autonomy and judicial privileges for centuries before Buchhorn was formally mediatised and incorporated into the Kingdom of Württemberg in 1802. \n\n Status: Free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Buchhorn; Common languages: Swabian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Urban council; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Württemberg

name: Free Imperial City of Lindau
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Lindau secured its imperial freedom from King Rudolf I of Habsburg in 1275, establishing an autonomous merchant republic on a sheltered island in Lake Constance. Its patrician council commanded significant lacustrine shipping routes, facilitating lucrative exchanges between Upper Swabia, the Swiss cantons and northern Italy. The island commune fortified its perimeter against regional sieges and preserved its cherished imperial immediacy until the restructuring of the Holy Roman Empire led to Bavarian annexation in 1804. \n\n Status: Free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Lindau; Common languages: Swabian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Urban republic; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Bavaria

name: Free Imperial City of Mulhouse
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Mulhouse acquired self-governing imperial immediacy in 1275 from King Rudolf I of Habsburg, breaking free from episcopal control in southern Alsace. Located in the Ill river basin, the city developed robust guild governance, flourishing textiles and lively cross-Rhine commercial partnerships. Under mounting aristocratic intimidation from neighbouring Habsburg dynasts, the burghers forged mutual defensive pacts with the Swiss cantons, eventually concluding an eternal alliance with the Swiss Confederation in 1515. \n\n Status: Free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Mulhouse; Common languages: Alsatian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Urban republic; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Swiss Confederation

name: Free Imperial City of Weil der Stadt
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Weil der Stadt gained imperial immediacy in the late thirteenth century, establishing an autonomous municipal commonwealth in the Würm river valley at the edge of the Black Forest. Guided by a local magistrate council, the town maintained civic independence, craft guilds and traditional market privileges. Despite surrounding Protestant conversions and repeated military pressures from the neighbouring Duchy of Württemberg, Weil preserved its imperial autonomy and Catholic faith until mediatisation in 1802. \n\n Status: Free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Weil der Stadt; Common languages: Swabian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Urban republic; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Württemberg

name: Sahip Ataids
label: anatolian beyliks
description: The Sahip Ataids constituted an autonomous Turkmen principality established around 1275 by the descendants of Fakhr al-Din Ali, the illustrious vizier of the Sultanate of Rum. Centred at the formidable crag citadel of Kara Hisar-i Sahib, modern Afyonkarahisar, the beylik governed strategic junction points linking western Anatolian highlands with central plateaus. The ruling beys patronised exquisite Seljuk-style religious architecture and madrasas until the territory was peacefully absorbed by the neighbouring Germiyanids in the 1340s. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Afyonkarahisar; Common languages: Old Anatolian Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sahipataoğulları; Ruler title: Bey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Sultanate of Rum; Succeeded by: Germiyanids

name: Signoria of Ravenna
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Ravenna was established in 1275 when Guido I da Polenta seized effective political control of the historic Adriatic city-state. Governing as hereditary lords, the da Polenta family fostered intellectual culture, famously sheltering the exiled poet Dante Alighieri in Ravenna during his final years. The signoria skilfully navigated shifting alliances between the Papacy, neighbouring Romagnol tyrants and the Republic of Venice before the Venetians definitively annexed the territory into their mainland dominion in 1441. \n\n Status: Sovereign signoria; Capital: Ravenna; Common languages: Romagnol and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Princely signoria; Ruling dynasty: Da Polenta; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Republic of Venice

name: Free Imperial City of Augsburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Augsburg attained autonomy from its prince-bishop in 1276 through a royal charter granted by King Rudolf I of Habsburg. Situated at the confluence of the Lech and Wertach rivers, Augsburg developed into one of the wealthiest financial and commercial centres in Europe, anchored by legendary merchant dynasties like the Fuggers and Welsers. The city hosted momentous imperial diets and fostered religious coexistence under parity arrangements before being mediatised into Bavaria in 1806. \n\n Status: Free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Augsburg; Common languages: Swabian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Urban republic; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Bavaria

name: Free Imperial City of Ravensburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Ravensburg secured imperial immediacy in 1276, developing into a premier mercantile republic in the Upper Swabian region. Its prominent merchant patriciate established the Great Ravensburg Trading Society, conducting widespread pan-European commerce in textiles, paper and spices. Enclosed by formidable stone towers and gatehouses, the municipal government exercised sovereign jurisdiction until the upheavals of the Napoleonic period brought the city first to Bavaria and later to the Kingdom of Württemberg. \n\n Status: Free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Ravensburg; Common languages: Swabian German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Urban republic; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Bavaria

name: Kingdom of al-Abwab
label: christian kingdoms of nubia
description: The Kingdom of al-Abwab was an autonomous Christian Nubian monarchy that formed along the Middle Nile near the confluence with the Atbara River. Formerly the northern frontier march of Alodia, the kingdom seceded into full sovereignty under King Adur during escalating regional hostilities in the late thirteenth century. Controlling the narrow river defiles known as the Gates of Nubia, the state repulsed surrounding tribal raids and asserted independent regional leadership before increasing Egyptian diplomatic and military influence intervened. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: al-Abwab; Common languages: Old Nubian; Religion: Coptic Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Alodia; Succeeded by: Funj Sultanate

name: Kingdom of Navarre
description: The Kingdom of Navarre entered into a personal union with the Capetian Kingdom of France following the marriage of Queen Joan I to Philip IV the Fair in the late thirteenth century. Governed through royal seneschals from Pamplona, the Pyrenean kingdom retained its distinctive legal customs, fueros and regional Cortes while sharing monarchs with the French crown. This transatlantic union endured until the death of Charles IV in 1328, whereupon the Navarrese crown passed separately to Joan II. \n\n Status: Monarchy in personal union with the Kingdom of France; Capital: Pamplona; Common languages: Basque, Gascon and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Capetian; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Navarre

name: Lordship of Homburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Homburg was an immediate imperial territory of the Holy Roman Empire located in the Bergisches Land of western Germany. Centred upon the fortified hill fortress of Schloss Homburg near Nümbrecht, the lordship was held by dynasts of the House of Sayn-Wittgenstein. The lords exercised territorial sovereignty, collected tolls and administered local justice across surrounding parishes until the lordship was mediatised into the Grand Duchy of Berg during the Napoleonic reorganisation of 1806. \n\n Status: Imperial lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Nümbrecht; Common languages: German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Reformed; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruling dynasty: House of Sayn-Wittgenstein; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Berg

name: Sultanate of Rum
description: The Sultanate of Rum entered a fleeting period of vassalage under the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt following Sultan Baibars' stunning victory over Ilkhanid Mongol forces at the Battle of Elbistan in April 1277. Entering the Seljuk capital of Konya, Baibars received formal oaths of submission from local notables and Seljuk officials eager to escape Mongol hegemony. Mamluk overrule proved transitory, however, as logistical strains prompted an early Egyptian withdrawal, allowing the Ilkhanate to swiftly reassert its dominance over central Anatolia. \n\n Status: Vassal sultanate of the Mamluk Sultanate; Capital: Konya; Common languages: Persian and Old Anatolian Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic sultanate; Ruling dynasty: Seljuk; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Sultanate of Rum; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Rum

name: Kingdom of al-Abwab
label: christian kingdoms of nubia
description: The Kingdom of al-Abwab came under the tributary overlordship of Mamluk Egypt around 1278 as Cairo intervened actively in Nubian geopolitical conflicts. Positioned near modern Shendi, King Adur and his successors collaborated with Mamluk expeditions operating against the neighbouring Christian Kingdom of Makuria to ensure their own political survival. Although paying periodic tribute to Cairo, the monarchy retained internal autonomy over its riverine chiefdoms until nomad migrations and the rise of the Funj Sultanate absorbed the realm. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Mamluk Sultanate; Capital: al-Abwab; Common languages: Old Nubian and Arabic; Religion: Coptic Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Funj Sultanate

name: Pervâneoğulları
label: anatolian beyliks
description: The Pervâneoğulları beylik was established along the northern Black Sea coast of Anatolia by the heirs of the powerful Seljuk statesman Mu'in al-Din Sulayman, known as the Pervane. Operating from the fortified peninsula port of Sinop, the dynasty developed a formidable regional navy that conducted maritime raids against the Empire of Trebizond and Genoese trade convoys. Under Gazi Çelebi, the principality commanded naval dominance in the Black Sea before dynastic succession disputes led to Candarid annexation in 1322. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Sinop; Common languages: Old Anatolian Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Pervaneids; Ruler title: Bey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Candarids

name: Principality of Mozhaisk
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Mozhaisk was an autonomous Russian domain established in the late thirteenth century around the upper reaches of the Moskva River. Serving as a crucial defensive barrier guarding western approaches towards Moscow, its ruling Rurikid princes maintained independent authority over local fortresses and trade corridors. In 1303, following Prince Svyatoslav Glebovich's defeat, Daniel of Moscow seized Mozhaisk and incorporated its lands, converting the border territory into a vital defensive bulwark of the expanding Muscovite realm. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Mozhaisk; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurikid; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Beylik of Eshref
label: anatolian beyliks
description: The Beylik of Eshref was an autonomous Turkmen principality established in southwestern central Anatolia by Seyfeddin Süleyman Bey in the late thirteenth century. Headquartered at Beyşehir on the eastern shore of Lake Beyşehir, the dynasty governed territory extending towards Seydişehir and Ilgın. name: County of Schaumburg

name: Commune of San Miniato

name: County of Holstein-Plön

name: Free Imperial City of Besançon

name: Free Imperial City of Goslar

name: Mandi State

Under Orhan and Murad I, the beylik crossed the Dardanelles into Thrace, establishing a second capital at Edirne and laying the foundations for an expansive transcontinental empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Söğüt, Bursa and Edirne; Common languages: Old Anatolian Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Osman; Ruler title: Bey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Sultanate of Delhi
description: The Sultanate of Delhi entered a dramatic phase of military expansion and administrative centralisation following the rise of the Turco-Afghan Khalji dynasty in 1290. Under Sultan Alauddin Khalji, the Delhi court decisively repulsed multiple Mongol invasions while launching audacious southern campaigns that subjugated the wealthy kingdoms of the Deccan and southern India. Alauddin instituted rigorous market regulations, tax reforms and military levies that consolidated imperial authority across the Indian subcontinent before dynastic instability enabled the Tughlaq takeover in 1320. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Delhi; Common languages: Persian and Hindavi; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic sultanate; Ruling dynasty: Khalji; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Mamluk dynasty of Delhi; Succeeded by: Tughlaq dynasty

name: Commune of Pola
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Pola was an autonomous maritime city-state situated at the southern extremity of the Istrian peninsula, clustered around its ancient Roman harbour and amphitheatre. In the late thirteenth century, local noble families such as the Castropola secured de facto communal self-government, resisting the secular jurisdiction of the Patriarchate of Aquileia. The commune defended its local commerce, shipbuilding yards and fisheries amidst turbulent Adriatic conflicts until the Republic of Venice intervened directly, annexing Pola into its maritime empire in 1331. \n\n Status: Free medieval commune; Capital: Pula; Common languages: Venetian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Communal republic; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Republic of Venice

name: Free Imperial City of Landau
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Landau gained imperial immediacy and municipal privileges in 1291 from King Rudolf I of Habsburg. Located in the fertile Palatinate plain east of the Palatinate Forest, the city flourished as an essential regional marketplace for wine, grain and manufactured goods along the Queich river. Landau zealously preserved its civic liberties through successive imperial pledges and joined the Alsatian Décapole in 1521, maintaining independent self-government until the geopolitical shifts of the Peace of Westphalia. \n\n Status: Free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Landau in der Pfalz; Common languages: Palatine German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Urban republic; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Décapole

name: Margraviate of Antwerp
label: holy roman empire
description: The Margraviate of Antwerp, also known as the March of Antwerp, was an imperial territory situated along the lower Scheldt River in the Low Countries. Originally created as a frontier march of the Holy Roman Empire to guard against western incursions, the margraviate was governed from Antwerp and extended over Breda and the surrounding Campine. The margraves promoted deep-water port facilities and granted commercial privileges that transformed Antwerp into a burgeoning international trade emporium before its full integration into Brabant. \n\n Status: Imperial margraviate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Antwerp; Common languages: Middle Dutch; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal margraviate; Ruler title: Margrave of Antwerp; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Lower Lotharingia; Succeeded by: Duchy of Brabant

name: Swiss Confederacy
label: holy roman empire
description: The Swiss Confederacy, historically designated the Old Swiss Confederacy, arose from the mutual defensive pact concluded in August 1291 between the forest cantons of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden. Expanding to incorporate prosperous city-states like Zurich and Bern, this league of autonomous rural and urban communes successfully defeated repeated Habsburg armies and secured de facto independence within the Holy Roman Empire. The confederates coordinated foreign policy and common military defence through the federal Tagsatzung, maintaining their sovereign liberties until the French invasion of 1798. \n\n Status: Sovereign confederation; Capital: Zürich; Common languages: Alemannic German, French and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Reformed; Government: Confederation of cantons; Legislature: Tagsatzung; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Succeeded by: Helvetic Republic

name: Beylik of Jandar
label: anatolian beyliks
description: The Beylik of Jandar, ruled by the Candarid or Isfendiyarid dynasty, was established in 1291 by Şemseddin Yaman Candar in the ancient Paphlagonian region of northern Anatolia. Governed successively from Eflani, Kastamonu and the Black Sea port of Sinop, the beylik maintained a powerful regional navy and exploited lucrative copper and iron mines. Candarid rulers balanced diplomacy with the Byzantines, Trebizond and expanding Ottoman rivals until Sultan Mehmed II conquered the principality and incorporated it into the Ottoman Empire in 1461. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Eflani, Kastamonu and Sinop; Common languages: Old Anatolian Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Candarids; Ruler title: Bey; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Sultanate of Rum; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Chiang Hung State
label: shan states
description: Chiang Hung State, known natively as Moeng Lü or Sipsong Panna, was an autonomous Tai Lü kingdom nestled along the upper Mekong River in the borderlands of southern Yunnan. Confronted by the southward expansion of the Mongol Yuan dynasty, the ruling house submitted to imperial suzerainty in 1293, receiving recognition as a tributary frontier chieftaincy. The local monarchs preserved internal mandala administration over their twelve rice-growing federations from the capital of Chiang Hung, balancing relations with neighbouring Shan and Thai kingdoms. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Yuan Empire; Capital: Chiang Hung; Common languages: Tai Lü; Religion: Theravada Buddhism and Animism; Government: Mandala monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Pagna Jueang; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Cheli Tusi

name: Lan Na Kingdom
description: The Lan Na Kingdom was established in northern Thailand in 1292 by King Mangrai, who consolidated Tai city-states and founded the fortified capital of Chiang Mai in the Ping river basin. Operating as an autonomous mandala kingdom, Lan Na developed a distinctive northern Thai culture characterised by exquisite Buddhist monastic architecture, refined palm-leaf literature and codified secular statutes. The realm repulsed early Mongol incursions and flourished as an independent regional power before succumbing to Burmese vassalage under the Toungoo dynasty in 1558. \n\n Status: Sovereign mandala kingdom; Capital: Chiang Mai; Common languages: Lanna, Tai Lue and Old Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Mandala monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Mangrai; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Early Modern; Preceded by: Ngoenyang; Succeeded by: Toungoo dynasty

name: Narsinghpur State
description: Narsinghpur State was an autonomous princely realm situated along the scenic valley of the Mahanadi River in central Odisha. Founded in the late thirteenth century by Rajput dynasts who established their fortified headquarters at Narsinghpur, the state was bordered by dense forest ranges and neighbouring Orissan estates. The ruling rajas governed under traditional Hindu customary laws, patronising local temple rituals and defending their agrarian domains against Maratha raiding expeditions until the British East India Company established paramountcy over Odisha. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Narsinghpur; Common languages: Odia; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rajput; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Late Middle Ages to Modern; Succeeded by: British East India Company
